3331.title: Social Interactivity
3331.heading: Social Interactivity
3331.content:
Social interactivity arises from relationships among players or between players and socially legible agents. It includes communication, grouping, reciprocity, complementary roles, competition, and cooperation.

These loops often develop more slowly than moment-to-moment action and can extend outside a single play session through [[Metagaming]]. Social systems remain engaging while relationships and group positions can still change meaningfully.

3334.title: Social Honeypot
3334.heading: Social Honeypot
3334.content:
A social honeypot is a legitimate-looking account created to attract suspicious interactions. Accounts that send deceptive information or malicious links to it become candidates for labeling and later supervised detection.

Honeypots obtain labels cheaply but passively, so collection may take a long time. They also emphasize malicious positive examples and require another method to represent normal accounts accurately.

3337.title: Social Engineering
3337.heading: Social Engineering
3337.content:
Social engineering manipulates people into disclosing information, granting access, or performing an unsafe action. Instead of defeating a technical control directly, the attacker exploits trust, urgency, authority, curiosity, or another predictable human response.

Technical defenses alone cannot eliminate this attack path. Verification procedures, training, limited privileges, and multiple layers of control help keep one persuaded user from compromising an entire system.

Context makes recommendation more than a lookup of similar items. It explains how an identical item can receive different responses depending on receivers, senders, and their prior history.

3343.title: Social Explanation of AI Decisions
3343.heading: Social Explanation of AI Decisions
3343.content:
A social explanation of an AI decision treats explanation as an answer given by one party to another in a particular context. The affected person usually asks not for every calculation, but why this outcome occurred, what evidence mattered, how it compares with alternatives, and what can be challenged.

Explanations are therefore audience-sensitive and connected to responsibility. A technical account for a developer, an audit record for a regulator, and a reason given to an applicant may all be valid at different levels. [[Explainable AI]] succeeds ethically when it supports understanding and action rather than merely increasing the volume of disclosed information.

3346.title: Social Computing
3346.heading: Social Computing
3346.content:
Social computing describes systems that serve as a medium or focus for social relationships. As a medium, a system supports existing social conventions and contexts. As a focus, it creates new forms of social activity that would not otherwise occur.

Because conversations and conventions are situated in social reality, social computing is a form of [[Embodied Interaction]]. It is closely related to [[Computer-Supported Cooperative Work]], which concentrates on supporting collaborative activities and their coordination.

In three-dimensional environments, social computing can place remote users in a shared virtual space through [[Telepresence]].

Conversational assistants can also become social actors rather than neutral communication channels. Voice, timing, memory, and [[Assistant Personality]] invite people to apply social expectations to a [[Social Virtual Assistant]] or [[Social Robot]], even when the system's actual understanding is narrow.

3349.title: Social Bot
3349.heading: Social Bot
3349.content:
A social bot is an automated or partially automated account that participates in an online social system. Bots can provide benign services or manipulate attention, conversation, and apparent consensus.

Detection is difficult because behavior ranges from simple automation to coordinated, human-like activity. Feature engineering combines account, content, temporal, and network evidence rather than relying on a single visible cue.

3351.sourceSearchName: social bot user feature social bot user feature
3351.title: Social Bot User Feature

3352.sourceSearchName: social bot user feature social bot user feature
3352.title: Social Bot User Feature
3352.heading: Social Bot User Feature
3352.content:
A social bot user feature derives from profile and account attributes such as age, description, counts, or interface settings. These variables summarize how an account presents itself and its accumulated platform activity.

User features are inexpensive and interpretable, but sophisticated bots can imitate normal profiles. They are strongest when combined with behavioral and relational evidence.

3355.sourceSearchName: social bot temporal feature social bot temporal feature
3355.title: Social Bot Temporal Feature
3355.heading: Social Bot Temporal Feature
3355.content:
A social bot temporal feature summarizes when and how regularly an account acts. Posting intervals, daily rhythms, bursts, and response timing can expose scheduling or machine-speed behavior.

Automation does not always mean constant or perfectly regular activity, and humans can also show routines. Temporal evidence is therefore more reliable as part of a multi-family representation.

3358.heading: Social Bot Network Feature
3358.content:
A social bot network feature describes structural or interaction relationships involving an account. Retweet, mention, and hashtag co-occurrence networks provide different views of how it participates in information flow.

Network measures can expose coordination, centrality, and neighborhood patterns. Each network definition encodes a different behavior, so combining them requires attention to scale and meaning.

3361.heading: Social Bot Friend Feature
3361.content:
A social bot friend feature summarizes properties of the accounts connected to a focal user. Aggregates over followers or friends can expose an unusual social environment even when the focal profile appears ordinary.

These features extend detection beyond self-reported attributes. Sampling limits, private accounts, and coordinated manipulation can affect the reliability of friend-based summaries.

3364.heading: Social Bot Content Feature
3364.content:
A social bot content feature is derived from the language and symbols used in an account's posts. Word usage, parts of speech, entities, hashtags, links, and repetition can characterize automated production.

Content features capture what an account says, but language varies by topic, community, and time. Robust detection separates automation signals from ordinary topical differences.

3367.title: Snake Lemma
3367.heading: Snake Lemma
3367.content:
The Snake Lemma starts from a commutative diagram with exact rows and constructs a connecting homomorphism between a kernel and a cokernel. These objects fit into one longer exact sequence.

It systematically relates the failures of injectivity and surjectivity of the vertical maps. The connecting map is obtained by following representatives through the diagram and checking that choices do not change the resulting class.

3370.content:
A SOAP web service exchanges structured messages according to the Simple Object Access Protocol. SOAP defines an application-level messaging contract above the transport and is commonly carried through HTTP rather than replacing HTTP's network role.

The contract can standardize operations and message structure across consumers, but its additional envelope and service conventions are useful only when both sides need that formal interoperability.

3373.sourceSearchName: snell s law snell s law
3373.title: Snell's Law
3373.heading: Snell's Law
3373.content:
Snell's law relates refraction angles and refractive indices at a boundary:

$$n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2.$$

Frequency remains continuous across the boundary, while wave speed and wavelength change. A wave bends toward the normal when it enters a medium with larger refractive index and lower phase speed.

3376.title: SMOTE Oversampling
3376.heading: SMOTE Oversampling
3376.content:
SMOTE oversampling creates synthetic minority observations along line segments joining a rare-class case to selected rare-class neighbors. It expands the minority region without merely copying the same examples.

The method can help a classifier form a broader boundary around sparse positives, but synthetic points may cross into majority territory when classes overlap. Neighborhood choice and the amount of oversampling therefore require validation.

3379.title: Smoothing
3379.heading: Smoothing
3379.content:
Smoothing revises an estimate of a past hidden state by using observations that occurred after that state. Later evidence can distinguish past explanations that were difficult to separate at the time.

It is the backward-looking counterpart to prediction in a time-indexed Bayesian model. Smoothing therefore requires retaining or reconstructing information beyond the single current filtered belief.

A smartphone combines a personal computer with cellular radio, Wi-Fi, cameras, satellite positioning, audio, video, motion sensors, and touch interaction. The microprocessor turns their input signals into software-defined capabilities.

The device exemplifies convergence, but its networks and interfaces remain constrained by carrier policy, screen size, power, and incompatible access systems. Integration is therefore technical and institutional.

3388.title: Smoke Test
3388.heading: Smoke Test
3388.content:
A smoke test is a fast, broad check that a build loads and begins running without an immediate critical failure. For a multiplatform game, the check is performed on every supported platform and relevant build configuration.

It supplies a cheap gate before slower tests or playthroughs. Passing proves basic viability, not full correctness or playability.

3391.sourceSearchName: smart device security smart device security
3391.title: Smart Device Security
3391.heading: Smart Device Security
3391.content:
Smart device security protects connected consumer and embedded products whose computation is tied to a physical function. These devices may collect sensitive information, accept remote commands, and remain deployed longer than ordinary software support cycles.

Default credentials, limited update mechanisms, and weak visibility can turn a convenient product into a [[Cyber Vulnerability]]. Device identity, secure configuration, updates, network isolation, and lifecycle support are therefore essential.

Shared class boundaries and palettes are essential when color must have the same meaning in every panel. The layout becomes ineffective when panels are too small to preserve recognizable regions.

3397.heading: Slope of a Line
3397.content: The slope of the line through $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ is $m=(y_2-y_1)/(x_2-x_1)$ when $x_1\ne x_2$. It measures vertical change per unit of horizontal change. Positive and negative slopes distinguish rising and falling lines, zero describes a horizontal line, and a vertical line has undefined slope.

3400.title: Slack Variable
3400.heading: Slack Variable
3400.content:
A slack variable converts a less-than-or-equal [[Linear Constraint]] into an equality by recording unused capacity. For $a^Tx\leq b$, adding $s\geq0$ gives $a^Tx+s=b$.

Slack variables often form the initial basis of a simplex tableau. A zero slack value means the associated constraint is binding.

3403.content:
A sliding-window sequence feature applies a pattern-matching summary within successive local windows. The resulting values describe how pattern activity changes along the sequence.

Window length and stride determine temporal or positional resolution. Short overlapping windows preserve locality but increase dimensionality and dependence among neighboring features.

3406.sourceSearchName: sky augmentation versus extraction sky augmentation versus extraction
3406.title: Sky Augmentation versus Extraction
3406.heading: Sky Augmentation versus Extraction
3406.content: A flat, nearly uniform sky may be improved by laying a new sky plate over it and masking that plate just above the horizon, rather than extracting every foreground boundary. Edge feather and reduced opacity let the two skies blend. A more complex sky or horizon demands roto, paint, or a procedural extraction to separate scene elements. In either case, the new sky's sun direction and atmospheric color must agree with the ground plate; the book flips a cloud plate when its light direction conflicts with shadows. See [[Feathering a Composite Edge]].

3409.title: Skinning Matrix Palette
3409.heading: Skinning Matrix Palette
3409.content:
A skinning matrix palette is the array of current bone skinning transforms supplied to the GPU. Each entry combines a bone's [[Inverse Bind Pose Matrix]] with its global transform in the current [[Animation Pose]].

Vertex bone indices select entries from the palette, and weights blend their transformed results. The palette is updated when the animation pose changes rather than recomputed independently for every vertex.

3412.title: Skin Weight
3412.heading: Skin Weight
3412.content:
A skin weight states how strongly one skeletal bone influences a mesh vertex. A vertex commonly stores several bone indices and nonnegative weights whose total is normalized to one.

Vertices near a joint blend neighboring bone transforms, producing a smoother bend than rigid attachment to one bone. The number of influences is limited so [[Vertex Skinning]] remains efficient and fits the vertex format.

3415.heading: Skill Strategy Chance and Uncertainty as Design Values
3415.content:
A design should state the intended balance among practiced skill, forward-looking strategy, randomized events, and uncertainty from hidden or interacting causes. Each produces a different basis for success and a different emotional rhythm.

Making the balance explicit prevents one source from erasing the others. Excessive randomness can make developed skill irrelevant, while complete predictability can eliminate the uncertainty that gives strategic commitment its tension.

3418.title: Skill-Based Play
3418.heading: Skill-Based Play
3418.content:
Skill-based play centers satisfaction on developing and applying a capacity that improves with practice. Active skill concerns timing, coordination, dexterity, and other embodied performance; mental skill concerns memory, inference, calculation, planning, or pattern recognition.

A skill becomes part of the game only when its consequences are perceptible. Clear [[Feedback]] lets players connect practice to improved performance and distinguish a demanding challenge from arbitrary failure.

3421.title: Skill Acquisition
3421.heading: Skill Acquisition
3421.content:
Skill acquisition is the process through which repeated performance makes actions faster, more accurate, and less dependent on conscious attention.

The cognitive stage relies on explicit instructions and deliberate thought. The associative stage tunes behavior and reduces errors. In the autonomous stage, actions can be executed rapidly and accurately with little conscious control. Acquired skills are stored as procedural knowledge in [[Long-Term Memory]].

For training in a [[Virtual Environment]], an important question is whether a skill learned through the interface transfers to performance in the physical world.

3424.title: Skew-Symmetric Matrix
3424.heading: Skew-Symmetric Matrix
3424.content:
A real square matrix is skew-symmetric when $A^T=-A$. Every diagonal entry must therefore be zero.

The condition is checked by comparing corresponding entries across the main diagonal: $a_{ij}=-a_{ji}$. This distinguishes skew symmetry from the mirrored equality of a [[Symmetric Matrix]].

3427.title: Skeleton Hierarchy
3427.heading: Skeleton Hierarchy
3427.content:
A skeleton hierarchy organizes animation bones as a tree. Every bone except the root has a parent, so a local bone transform is interpreted relative to the parent's current transform.

Global transforms are calculated from the root outward by concatenating each local pose with the parent's global pose. Parent-before-child ordering is therefore essential when evaluating an [[Animation Pose]].

3429.sourceSearchName: skeletal muscle actuator skeletal muscle actuator
3429.title: Skeletal Muscle Actuator

3430.sourceSearchName: skeletal muscle actuator skeletal muscle actuator
3430.title: Skeletal Muscle Actuator
3430.heading: Skeletal Muscle Actuator
3430.content:
A skeletal muscle actuator uses aligned myotubes to generate voluntary-style contraction on demand. Electrical or optical stimulation activates the tissue, and attachment across a flexible joint converts shortening into motion.

The actuator can be trained by repeated stimulation and can produce directional control, but it requires maturation, anchoring, and continued access to culture medium.

3433.title: Skeletal Animation Bone
3433.heading: Skeletal Animation Bone
3433.content:
A skeletal animation bone is a rigid coordinate frame within a [[Skeleton Hierarchy]]. It stores a parent relationship and a local transform describing its position and orientation relative to that parent.

The bone does not render as visible geometry. Instead, vertices reference one or more bones through [[Skin Weight|skin weights]], allowing the animated hierarchy to deform the surrounding mesh.

3436.heading: Skeletal Animation Interpolation
3436.content:
Skeletal animation interpolation constructs a pose between two sampled animation frames. Translation is blended linearly, while rotation uses quaternion interpolation so orientation follows a meaningful path without Euler-angle discontinuities.

The same fraction must be applied across corresponding bones to produce a coherent pose. Interpolation smooths playback when the render or update rate differs from the stored [[Animation Clip]] sampling rate.

3439.title: Six Dimensions of Computational Thinking
3439.heading: Six Dimensions of Computational Thinking
3439.content:
Computational thinking can be viewed through six dimensions: methods, machines, computing education, software engineering, design, and computational science. Each highlights a different practice through which people formulate, execute, teach, scale, evaluate, or investigate computations.

The dimensions overlap without collapsing into one another. Together they connect the ancient history of calculation with modern computing systems and show why computational thinking is richer than programming alone.

3442.title: Situation Awareness
3442.heading: Situation Awareness
3442.content:
Situation awareness is an internal model of the current state of a user's environment. It includes perceiving relevant elements across time and space, understanding their meaning, and projecting how their status may change in the near future.

The model can include spatial relationships, other users, and task states, making it a basis for [[Decision-Making]]. In [[Navigation]], situation awareness depends on both spatial orientation—knowing one's location and viewing direction—and [[Spatial Knowledge]] stored in a [[Cognitive Map]].

A 3D interface can support situation awareness with overviews, landmarks, maps, and clearly managed viewpoint changes.

Mobile AR can add registered information about relevant objects while allowing the user to continue looking at the physical surroundings. This can improve discovery and awareness, but excessive or poorly placed augmentation can also cover the evidence the user needs to perceive the situation directly.

3445.title: Situational Leadership
3445.heading: Situational Leadership
3445.content:
Situational leadership adjusts the balance of direction and support to a team's capability and confidence. A leader may direct an inexperienced group, coach developing competence, support capable people who need confidence, and delegate to a mature team.

The goal is not permanent control but the least intervention that helps the team succeed and grow toward self-management.

3448.heading: Singular Value Spectrum
3448.content:
A singular value spectrum is the ordered collection of singular values from a [[Singular Value Decomposition]]. Squared singular values quantify how much sum-of-squares variation lies along the corresponding transformed directions.

A steep spectrum indicates that a small number of directions capture much of the dataset's structure. A gradual spectrum warns that aggressive reduction will discard substantial variation and distort distances or reconstruction.

3451.title: Situated Annotation
3451.heading: Situated Annotation
3451.content:
A situated annotation attaches explanatory information to the physical object, place, or feature it describes. Registration reduces the need to translate between a separate document and the observed environment.

The annotation may be text, graphics, or a link to additional content. Its placement must remain legible as viewpoint and occlusion change, and its visual relationship must make the intended referent unambiguous.

3454.heading: Singular Value Decomposition
3454.content:
Singular value decomposition factors a real matrix as $A=UDV^T$, where $U$ and $V$ are orthogonal and $D$ is diagonal or rectangular diagonal with nonnegative singular values.

Unlike eigenvalue decomposition, SVD applies to rectangular matrices. It exposes rank and conditioning and provides stable formulas for the [[Pseudoinverse]] and [[Least Squares Approximation]].

For high-dimensional data, the source orders the transformed directions by decreasing sum of squares. Retaining the leading directions creates a lower-dimensional approximation that preserves dominant variation and often preserves much of the pairwise distance among samples.

3457.title: Singular Matrix
3457.heading: Singular Matrix
3457.content:
A singular matrix is a [[Square Matrix]] with zero [[Determinant]]. It has no [[Matrix Inverse]] and does not have full [[Matrix Rank]].

For $Ax=0$, singularity permits nonzero solutions. In numerical methods it may also prevent a factorization step or triangular solve from producing a unique solution.

3460.title: Singleton Pattern
3460.heading: Singleton Pattern
3460.content:
The singleton pattern constrains a class to one instance within a chosen application boundary. The book uses a single inventory context so commands observe the same in-memory book collection, then shows how a .NET service container can manage that lifetime. One instance is not the same as thread safety: concurrent mutation still requires coordination. A singleton can also hide global state and create a bottleneck, so it should be used only when shared identity is a real requirement.

Singleton centralizes access to one class instance across an application, but instance count alone does not make the object's state safe or its lifetime appropriate. The source's connection-configuration example illustrates the wish for one source of settings, which is distinct from requiring only one physical database connection.

3463.heading: Single-Slit Diffraction
3463.content: Single-slit diffraction spreads a wave after it passes through an aperture comparable to its wavelength. Destructive minima for slit width $a$ satisfy $a\sin\theta=m\lambda$ for nonzero integer $m$. The central maximum is twice the angular width of the neighboring maxima, and narrowing the slit broadens the pattern.

3466.title: Singleton Service
3466.heading: Singleton Service
3466.content:
A singleton service has one shared instance within an application. Angular can provide a service at the application root so every injected consumer receives that same instance.

This avoids creating redundant service objects and is the common arrangement for stateless API access or intentionally shared state. A service need not be a singleton, so its provider scope remains a design decision.

.NET Core's `AddSingleton` registration similarly provides one service instance per built service provider. The book's inventory tests show why the provider boundary matters: building a new provider for every resolution produces a new singleton in each provider. A shared instance may still need synchronization when several threads mutate it.

3469.content:
A single-page application loads one main HTML document and uses client-side code to change the visible interface and request data as the user works. It aims for desktop-like responsiveness without requiring a complete page reload for each interaction.

The pattern separates data, business behavior, and presentation, transfers much of the UI to the browser, and uses [[Angular Routing]] to preserve navigation state. It still depends on a [[Web Server]] and usually communicates with a [[Web API]].

A single-provider cloud usage model places one IT service provider between the organization's business units and delivered services. A central IT department controls contracts and service agreements, while the provider may subcontract parts of delivery.

The arrangement gives a clear accountability path but tightly couples business demand to the central function and provider. That control can make it slow to adopt a different service when requirements change.

Single-link clustering defines the distance between two clusters by the nearest pair of observations across them. It is also called nearest-neighbor linkage.

This rule can recover elongated or irregular chains because one close bridge is enough to join groups. The same property can cause chaining, where otherwise distinct dense groups connect through intermediate points.

3478.heading: Single-Image Depth Ambiguity
3478.content:
Single-image depth ambiguity arises because every image point corresponds to an entire ray of possible three-dimensional locations. Scaling a point's lateral position and depth by the same factor leaves its projected position unchanged, so one photograph alone cannot uniquely recover absolute scene geometry.

This ambiguity explains how a small nearby object can resemble a large distant one and why reconstruction requires additional constraints. Known dimensions, parallelism, support surfaces, anatomical proportions, or multiple views can narrow the family of scenes consistent with the image.

3481.heading: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping
3481.content:
Simultaneous localization and mapping builds a representation of an initially unknown environment while estimating the camera's pose within that representation. Tracked image features become landmarks, and new observations extend or refine both the map and the trajectory.

Incremental operation supports unprepared spaces but accumulates uncertainty and can lose tracking. Relocalization recovers a known pose, loop closure recognizes a previously mapped area, and bundle adjustment jointly improves camera and landmark estimates.

3484.heading: Single Responsibility Principle
3484.content:
The single responsibility principle gives a class one coherent reason to change. When user interaction, business rules, and storage concerns all reside in one class, a change in any one area can disturb the others. Separating those responsibilities makes each component easier to understand and test, provided the split follows real change boundaries rather than producing many trivial wrappers.

One practical test is whether a class has more than one independent reason to change. When unrelated responsibilities share a class, modifying one concern can disturb dependencies belonging to the other and make the code harder to isolate.

3493.title: Simulation
3493.heading: Simulation
3493.content:
A simulation executes a [[Computational Model]] to track how a represented system changes over time or across states. Variables, equations, parameters, and transition rules determine the behavior that can emerge.

Simulation makes complex models explorable, but it produces evidence about the modeled system rather than direct observation of reality. Credibility requires verification of the implementation and validation against independent knowledge of the phenomenon.

3496.content:
Simulation geometry defeaturing removes small holes, fillets, chamfers, sliver faces, spikes, or other production detail that degrades mesh quality without contributing meaningfully to the modeled physics. Fewer small entities can reduce element count and solver difficulty.

Defeaturing must be selective because a visually minor feature may create a stress concentration, flow separation, contact, or thermal resistance central to the question. The removed feature and justification should remain documented.

3499.heading: Simulation Game
3499.content:
A simulation game models a process, activity, or system so the player can operate or explore it. Vehicle simulations emphasize control of a machine, while construction and management simulations emphasize building and managing processes under constraints.

The design abstracts reality selectively. Accuracy matters only to the degree needed for the intended experience, audience, and challenge; unnecessary detail can make the simulation less playable without making it more informative.

3502.content:

3508.heading: Simplifying Rational Expressions
3508.content:
Simplifying a [[Rational Expression]] rewrites its numerator and denominator as products and cancels common nonzero factors. For example,

$$\frac{x^2-1}{x^2-2x+1}=\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-1)^2}=\frac{x+1}{x-1}.$$

Only complete factors can be cancelled; terms connected by addition cannot be removed independently. Values that made the original denominator zero remain excluded after simplification. The factored form therefore reveals both cancellation opportunities and domain restrictions.

A simply supported beam is restrained against transverse displacement at its supports while remaining free to rotate. The support conditions create reactions but do not impose end moments in the ideal model.

In finite element equations, the supported displacement degrees of freedom are prescribed as zero and rotational degrees remain unknown. Symmetric loading and geometry can produce symmetric reactions and deflection.

3517.title: Simplex Method
3517.heading: Simplex Method
3517.content:
The simplex method solves a linear program by moving between basic feasible solutions represented in tableaus. At each iteration it selects an entering variable that can improve the objective and a leaving variable that preserves feasibility.

Pivot row operations update the basis. The process stops when the objective row shows that no permitted entering variable can improve the solution.

3520.title: Simple Pendulum
3520.heading: Simple Pendulum
3520.content: A simple pendulum is a point mass suspended by a light inextensible string. For small angular displacements, $\sin\theta\approx\theta$, making the restoring force proportional to displacement and the motion approximately harmonic. Its period is $T=2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$, independent of bob mass and approximately independent of amplitude only in the small-angle regime.

3523.heading: Simple Module
3523.content:
A simple module is a nonzero module whose only submodules are zero and itself. It cannot be decomposed further through a proper nontrivial submodule.

Every factor in a [[Composition Series]] is simple. Over a commutative ring, simple modules are represented by quotients R/m for [[Maximal Ideal]]s m.

3541.heading: Simple Feature
3541.content: A simple feature is a standardized representation of a geographic geometry and its attributes. 3544.title: Similarity Transformation
3544.heading: Similarity Transformation
3544.content:
A similarity transformation maps $A$ to $Q^{-1}AQ$ using a nonsingular matrix $Q$. It changes the coordinate representation while preserving the matrix's eigenvalues.

When $Q$ is an [[Orthogonal Matrix]], the transformation becomes $Q^TAQ$, which is easier and usually more stable to compute. [[Matrix Diagonalization]] is a special similarity transformation.

3547.heading: Similarity Graph for Spectral Clustering
3547.content:
A similarity graph represents observations as vertices and retains weighted edges between nearby or sufficiently similar pairs. It converts geometric data into a relational object on which spectral clustering operates.

Common constructions include full, epsilon-neighborhood, and k-nearest-neighbor graphs. Edge scale, connectivity, and weight function strongly affect the Laplacian spectrum, so graph construction is part of the clustering model rather than mere preprocessing.

3550.title: Similar Triangles
3550.heading: Similar Triangles
3550.content: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. Angle-angle information is sufficient to establish similarity, while side-angle-side and side-side-side proportionality provide other tests. Similarity preserves shape under scaling and supplies the geometric reason that [[Trigonometric Ratios]] depend only on an angle.

3553.title: Similar Matrices
3553.heading: Similar Matrices
3553.content:
Two square matrices $A$ and $B$ are similar when an invertible matrix $Q$ satisfies $B=Q^{-1}AQ$. They represent the same linear transformation in different coordinate bases.

Similar matrices have the same [[Characteristic Polynomial]], eigenvalues, determinant, and trace. Numerical eigenvalue algorithms exploit this by replacing a matrix with progressively simpler similar matrices.

3556.title: Silhouette Coefficient
3556.heading: Silhouette Coefficient
3556.content:
The silhouette value for an observation compares its average distance within its assigned cluster with its best average distance to another cluster, normalized by the larger of the two. Values near one favor the assignment, while negative values indicate a poorer fit than a competing cluster.

Averaging point values produces a silhouette coefficient for the clustering. Plotting it across candidate values of k can inform cluster-count selection.

3559.heading: Significant-Digit Override in the MATLAB Converter
3559.content: The Enhanced Unit Converter infers a default significant-digit count from the typed From value and limits that default to five because its factor precision varies. The book allows a Specify option to override the inference with up to seven digits when the user knows more about the input measurement. For example, a typed 1000 may be an estimate to the nearest thousand rather than four known digits; specifying one digit better reflects that context. 3562.title: Significant Figures
3562.heading: Significant Figures
3562.content: Significant figures communicate the precision justified by a measured quantity. Leading zeros locate the decimal point and are not significant, while zeros between nonzero digits are. A calculated result should not imply more precision than its least precise input; rounding should normally be postponed until the final value so intermediate truncation does not accumulate.

3565.title: Significant Digits in Unit Conversion
3565.heading: Significant Digits in Unit Conversion
3565.content: The meaningful digits of a converted result should reflect the precision known for the original measurement, not simply every digit produced by multiplying factors. Pryor's app applies a factor, chooses a significant-digit count, and rounds the result as separate steps. An exact defined factor does not improve the quality of the input observation, while a truncated derived factor may add its own limitation. The book's app also offers an override when its inference from entered digits does not represent the measurement's real accuracy. See [[Conversion Resolution versus Accuracy]].

3568.title: Significance Level
3568.heading: Significance Level
3568.content:
The significance level is the prespecified probability threshold used to control false rejection of a null hypothesis under its assumptions. A conventional value such as 0.05 becomes one input to power and sample-size planning.

Lowering the significance level while holding other inputs fixed requires more information or a larger effect to maintain the same [[Statistical Power]]. It should be set before viewing the results rather than moved until a preferred conclusion becomes significant.

3571.sourceSearchName: signature based threat detection signature based threat detection
3571.title: Signature-Based Threat Detection
3571.heading: Signature-Based Threat Detection
3571.content:
Signature-based threat detection compares observed code or behavior with known patterns associated with malicious activity. It is efficient when the harmful pattern has already been identified and encoded into a detection rule.

Its central limitation is novelty: a changed or previously unseen attack may not match a stored signature. This gap helps explain why a [[Zero-Day Attack]] and adaptive techniques such as a [[Behavioral Security Baseline]] require complementary defenses.

3574.title: SignalR
3574.heading: SignalR
3574.content:
SignalR is an ASP.NET Core library for real-time communication between server code and connected clients. Unlike a REST exchange initiated only by the client, it lets the server send a message when an event occurs.

A server exposes a hub and a React client creates a hub connection with named message handlers. This supplements rather than replaces REST: commands and resource retrieval can remain HTTP operations while notifications travel over the live connection.

The Azure chat project separates SignalR's programming model from its hosting infrastructure. The application still defines a hub and named client callbacks, while Azure SignalR Service manages the scalable connection layer used to broadcast chat and archive notifications.

3577.sourceSearchName: signal r service registration signal r service registration
3577.title: SignalR Service Registration
3577.heading: SignalR Service Registration
3577.content:
SignalR service registration adds the framework's real-time services to ASP.NET Core dependency injection and, in the book's 2019 project, chains the Azure SignalR integration onto that registration. The middleware configuration then maps the chat hub to a public route.

Registration and route mapping solve different parts of startup: one makes services available to application code, and the other places the hub in the HTTP pipeline. Static and default-file middleware can serve the browser client alongside the live endpoint.

3580.sourceSearchName: signal r server push signal r server push
3580.title: SignalR Server Push
3580.heading: SignalR Server Push
3580.content:
SignalR server push lets server-side code invoke named functions on connected clients without waiting for each client to poll for a change. The chat hub broadcasts a sender and message to every client as soon as its send method is called.

Push communication is useful for events whose value depends on timeliness, such as a new chat message or archive notification. The client must register a handler with the same event name and compatible arguments or the message cannot update its interface.

3583.title: SignalR JavaScript Client
3583.heading: SignalR JavaScript Client
3583.content:
The SignalR JavaScript client is the browser library that builds and starts a connection to an ASP.NET Core hub. The book installs the package with npm and copies the required client files into the application's public web root.

Client code attaches [[SignalR Client Handler|handlers]] before starting the connection and invokes [[SignalR Hub Method|hub methods]] for outbound actions. Its route and message names must match the server configuration exactly.
